<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README of the Mirra Backend project, here’s how to approach drawing an accurate and detailed system design diagram tailored to this umbrella application.

1. Project Overview & Purpose:
   • Mirra Backend is an umbrella Elixir project built by splitting concerns into multiple decoupled apps (modules). Each module has its own responsibility, from game logic and physics (Arena) to client rendering (Game Client), request routing (Gateway), game-specific logic (ChampionsOfMirra), persistence and shared game data (GameBackend), and configurations (Configurator). Several supporting/testing modules (e.g., arena_load_test and bot_manager) also exist.
   • The main purpose is to create a modular ecosystem where each game or service is independent yet can interact through well-defined integration points.

2. Main Components to Include:
   • Arena:
     - Handles core game logic, including player interactions and real-time game updates.
     - Contains a 2D physics engine (with native components in Rust for collision detection).
   • Game Client:
     - Renders the arena using simple 2D shapes and serves as a developer-friendly front-end.
     - Communicates primarily with the Arena.
   • Gateway:
     - Acts as the entry point for websocket connections.
     - Routes incoming messages to the appropriate game or service modules.
   • ChampionsOfMirra:
     - Contains game-specific logic (battle simulation, campaigns, items, units, users).
     - Integrates with general/shared logic provided by GameBackend.
   • GameBackend:
     - Central persistence and shared logic layer.
     - Manages data related to users, units, items, and configurations that other apps consume.
   • Configurator:
     - Provides a system for managing game configurations and feature flags.
     - Supports immutable configurations to enable rollbacks and A/B testing.
   • (Optional/Future) Additional apps like Bots, Matchmaking, Marketplace, Chat, Inventory, and Leaderboard that expand functionality.

3. Relationships and Interactions:
   • Draw directional arrows to show how:
     - Game Client sends user actions to Arena.
     - Arena receives actions, interacts with its native physics engine, and then broadcasts game updates.
     - Gateway connects external clients (via websockets) to the appropriate back-end (Arena, ChampionsOfMirra, GameBackend, etc.).
     - Game-specific modules (ChampionsOfMirra) rely on data and rules provided by GameBackend.
     - Configurator influences the behavior of all apps by managing game configurations and feature flags.
   • Note that many of these apps operate within the umbrella architecture, meaning interactions are typically done through function calls or internal messaging rather than REST/pipes. Still, drawing clear boundaries is valuable.

4. Architectural Patterns:
   • Emphasize modularity – each app is self-contained and communicates via defined interfaces.
   • Illustrate layering:
     - Presentation/client layer (Game Client)
     - Gateway/routing layer (Gateway)
     - Core game logic/physics layer (Arena)
     - Business and domain logic (ChampionsOfMirra, GameBackend)
     - Configuration management layer (Configurator)
   • Mark native modules such as the physics engine (in Arena/native and bot_manager/native) which are integrated for performance critical paths (collision detection, path finding).

5. Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Elixir/OTP for building the concurrent, fault-tolerant applications.
   • Protobuf for websocket message serialization (noting separate JS Protobuf in Game Client for front-end).
   • Nix and devenv – indicate these are used for reproducible environments and dependency management.
   • Docker (docker-compose) for containerized deployment.
   • Additionally, mention testing and CI/CD pipelines defined under the .github/workflows directory.
   • Highlight that native sub-components (written in Rust and managed via Cargo) illustrate how performance-critical modules are implemented.

6. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram:
   • Start by drawing containers (boxes) for each main component (Arena, Game Client, Gateway, ChampionsOfMirra, GameBackend, Configurator). Optionally, create sub-boxes or nested boxes to represent native modules (e.g., Arena’s physics engine, Bot Manager’s astar module).
   • Use clear labels on each box with the module/app name and, optionally, a short description of its responsibility.
   • Draw directional arrows to indicate the data flow:
       – From Game Client to Arena (player inputs, game state updates).
       – From Gateway to Arena and other apps (routing messages).
       – From game-specific modules (ChampionsOfMirra) to GameBackend (shared logic and persistence).
       – From Configurator to all components that rely on configuration changes.
   • Consider color coding:
       – One color for “front-end” or client components (Game Client),
       – A different color for communication layers (Gateway),
       – And other distinct colors for business logic and persistence layers.
   • Use shapes or annotations to differentiate between Elixir modules, native libraries (Rust/Cargo components), and configuration/deployment scripts (e.g., CI/CD workflows, Docker files).
   • Add external elements like the Nix and devenv ecosystem and CI/CD pipelines (GitHub workflows) if a high-level deployment/process diagram is desired.

7. Additional Tips:
   • Be as detailed as possible: Each component’s responsibilities and interactions should be captured.
   • Avoid excessive clutter by focusing on logical grouping – for instance, note that several apps are part of the umbrella but have clearly defined interfaces.
   • Use dashed or solid arrows to distinguish between synchronous calls (function invocations) and asynchronous messaging (pub/sub or event streams), if applicable.
   • A legend or key on the diagram can help explain the icons, colors, and arrow types chosen.

By following these instructions and tailoring the diagram to the inherent modularity of Mirra Backend, you’ll create a detailed and accurate system design diagram that reflects both the high-level architecture and the essential internal interactions of this complex, multi-app system.
</explanation>
